extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, students, and policymakers interested in freedom of expression, public discussion, and individual liberty
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical limits for freedom of opinion, freedom of action in self-regarding matters, and the social value of individuality, as articulated in a political-philosophical essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four grounds for freedom of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist four distinct grounds justifying the fullest liberty to form and express opinions: (1) a silenced opinion may be true (denying it assumes our infallibility); (2) even an error may contain a portion of truth that the prevailing opinion lacks; (3) if a true opinion is not vigorously contested it will be held as prejudice with little comprehension of its rational grounds; (4) the doctrine's meaning will be weakened and its vital effect lost unless it is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each ground is elaborated: openness prevents assuming infallibility; collision of adverse opinions supplies missing truth; contest preserves understanding and prevents dogmatic prejudice; contestation preserves the doctrine's practical effect on character and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion vs. action — when opinion loses immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions should be free, but lose immunity when expressed in circumstances that constitute positive instigation to mischievous acts (e.g., encouraging a mob).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: circulating that corn-dealers are starvers may be harmless in print but punishable if orally delivered to an excited mob before the dealer's house or handed as a placard among that mob. The distinction between mere expression and instigation to immediate harmful action governs permissibility and potential punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle for regulating action
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions (unlike mere opinions) which, without justifiable cause, do harm to others may and, in important cases, must be controlled by society; the individual 'must not make himself a nuisance to other people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom to act is allowed in matters concerning only the actor, 'so long as it is at their own risk and peril.' The individual's liberty to pursue experiments of living is valuable provided it does not injure others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for punishing instigation to tyrannicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Instigation to tyrannicide may be a proper subject of punishment only if an overt act has followed and at least a probable connection can be established between the instigation and the act; even then, only the government assailed can legitimately punish such attacks against its own existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes narrow conditions for criminal liability: mere advocacy is not enough; there must be overt action causally linked to the instigation, and punishment is a matter of self-defence by the government attacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of legally fixing bounds of 'temperate' expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to allow free expression 'on condition that the manner be temperate' are impracticable because it is impossible to fix where those bounds lie; offensiveness is often judged subjectively by those attacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that tests based on offence fail because a strong, effective attack will usually be perceived as intemperate by those who cannot answer it; therefore law cannot reliably enforce 'temperate' expression without arbitrary bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-discussion morality: avoid sophistry and misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal offences in debate are sophistical argument, suppression of facts or arguments, misstatement of the case, and misrepresentation of the opposite opinion; these are gravely objectionable but often done in good faith and are ill-suited for legal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such misconduct is frequently unintentional or done by the ignorant, it is rare to be able to label it morally culpable; therefore opinion and moral censure, rather than law, should address these faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal calumny and stigmatizing opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst offence of a polemic is to stigmatise those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men; calumny disproportionately harms those holding unpopular views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion (not law) should condemn malignity, bigotry, and intolerance in advocacy; advocates who fairly and honestly represent opponents deserve honour. Those with unpopular opinions generally succeed by studied moderation of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric harm of vituperation — special need to restrain attacks on minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Vituperation, invective, and sarcasm do more harm when used against comparatively defenceless or unpopular minorities than against prevailing opinion; therefore restraining such vituperation (socially, not legally) is more important when directed at the unprevailing side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that prevailing opinions gain unfair advantage when they employ vituperation, and that unpopular opinions can only obtain hearing through cautious, moderate language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to act in self-regarding matters and the value of experiments in living
rubrics_metrics.description: The same reasons for freedom of opinion require that men should be free to act upon their opinions in matters that concern only themselves; free scope should be given to varieties of character and experiments of living, short of injury to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing diverse ways of life permits practical testing of what works, fosters 'individuality' as an element of well-being, and contributes to social and moral progress. The proviso 'at their own risk and peril' is indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of cultivating individuality against conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual spontaneity and the development of personal desires, impulses, and judgment have intrinsic worth; conforming merely to custom or position dulls faculties and prevents moral and intellectual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and social arrangements should encourage people to use their faculties (observation, reasoning, judgment, firmness) by choosing for themselves; blind imitation produces no character, whereas self-directed choice exercises and strengthens mental and moral capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on individuality to protect others' rights and social development
rubrics_metrics.description: While individuality should be cultivated, it must be constrained 'to prevent the stronger specimens of human nature from encroaching on the rights of others'; compression necessary for preventing injury to others is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The loss to individual development from restraint is compensated by the better development of the social part of human nature and by protecting others' interests; restraint should be 'as much as necessary' but no more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong impulses as raw material for virtue, not a ground for suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong desires and impulses are not inherently evil; they are 'the raw material of human nature' which, when governed by a strong will and cultivated, are the source of great good as well as potential evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should not reject energetic natures because it cannot discipline them; instead, it should cultivate and direct energy into virtue via education and moral development rather than suppress it wholesale.
